utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, representing the defence for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo. Ms. Boler will be in the courtroom momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. (The witness entered court) .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that. MUHAMED VEJZAGIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I continue with my examination of this witness, I should like us to place our Exhibit D74/1, the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- if that could be placed on the easel so that he could use it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be in the courtroom as soon as the usher brings it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, towards the end of the afternoon yesterday, we had discussed the transformation of the former Yugoslav People's Army. So as to be able to continue with the questions, could you please remind us how the Yugoslav People's Army was transformed into army districts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was transformed towards the end of 1985 and, instead of armies based in the republics, each army was based in the capitals of the republics. Out of those armies, four military districts were formed, so that, after that transformation, we had the Zagreb, Belgrade, Split and Skopje military districts. There were no substantive reasons for this transformation. The aim was for the headquarters of army commands to be removed from under the influence of the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, parallel with the reorganisation of the army, did certain changes occur in the Territorial Defence, or, rather, did it strengthen or was it weakened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Parallel with the reorganisation of the operative army, measures were taken to transform the Territorial Defence as well. The Territorial Defence, as of 1985, the aim was to reduce it gradually every year so that I should like to show you, with the help of a table, this process of reduction in size of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A parallel process went on in all the other republics, so I would like to show you what the situation was at the beginning, that is, in 1985, and how it appeared at the end, that is, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now be given his expert report and this folder V1? (Handed). You are referring to your review contained in annex 1/4; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For us all to be able to follow, could this chart be placed under the ELMO, please? Could you explain it to us, please, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether this is functioning now -- can you see it? Here we see the numbers of the Territorial Defence forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period from 1985 to 1991. We see what the situation was on 31 December 1985. The Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, or should have had, 310,530 soldiers. The actual number present was 313,990. That was the situation on 31 December 1985. With the steps that were taken by Belgrade, the order was issued that the Territorial Defence should be reduced in size gradually every year so that, at the end, on 31 December 1991, the Territorial Defence was reduced -- sorry, in 1986 to 297,000; in 1987 to 292,000; in 1988 to 202,000; in 1989 to 298,000; in 1990 to 138,000 and, at the end, on 31 December 1991, the Territorial Defence had 86,000 soldiers, which means, in a period of five years, the number had been reduced from 313,900 to 86,164, which is a total reduction of 73 per cent, so the strength of the Territorial Defence was reduced by 73 per cent during this five-year period. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the next question, if this ends your answer to my previous question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on to say what you had in connection with the weakening of the Territorial Defence -- have you anything else to add in that connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was just one aspect of the weakening of the Territorial Defence. Other measures were also taken, so that, by decision of the general staff of 14 May 1990, the order was issued to take away the armaments from the Territorial Defence under the excuse that the warehouse in which the equipment was housed were not safe, but that was not the real reason. The real reason was that simultaneously with the reduction in the numbers of the Territorial Defence, it should also be disarmed, so that, by order of the supreme command, the total armaments of the Territorial Defence was collected and placed in the warehouses of the army. A part of the weaponry was left in the TO warehouses, but mostly in areas where the Serbs were in a majority, which meant that the Territorial Defence was virtually left without any weapons. Other measures were also taken to reduce the strength of the Territorial Defence and its efficiency. The first step taken was to reduce it in size, then to disarm it, then other measures were also taken. Its continued supply with up-to-date weaponry and equipment was also reduced. The intensity of the training of staff was also reduced, both of units and commands and staffs. Then, just before the war, a large quantity of documents was collected from TO staffs, so that war plans, mobilisation plans, contingency plans, all of these were taken away and they existed in the event that the Territorial Defence needed to be activated. Also, the plans for decoding were also collected, so that the original intention of using the Territorial Defence in the defence of the country was undermined.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, before I continue with my questions, let me repeat an observation that I made yesterday, because my colleagues are telling me that we should slow down a little for the interpreters to be able to keep up, and, secondly, after my question, will you wait for a minute and hear the English interpretation -- so could the usher give the witness another pair of headphones -- and only once you hear that the interpretation has been completed will you continue with your answer. I think it is a better idea to make this remark at the beginning than for our colleagues not to be able to follow. Thank you. You have been telling us about the reorganisation of the army and the weakening of the Territorial Defence. General, do you connect these facts to the preparations for what happened just before the outbreak of the crisis in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. These measures to reorganise the army and what was done to weaken the Territorial Defence corresponded to a political situation, a crisis, in the country, which came to a peak on 14 and 15 March and I will come back to that, when the general staff proposed the introduction of a state of emergency, but we will be coming back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, or, rather Brigadier, I am sorry, how did the military leadership in Belgrade act when it had already become obvious that the dissolution of the former SFRY was ongoing, especially after the independence of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period of time the Presidency was convened -- that was on 13 March 1991, the aim being that the Minister of the Army as you call it here in the west, the Federal Secretary for Defence in our case, General Kadijevic, was to propose the introduction of a state of emergency and the mobilisation of the reserve force. That proposal was reviewed by the presidency on that day, 13 March, and no consensus could be reached to adopt that proposal of the Federal Secretary, General Kadijevic. The representatives of Slovenia and then also of Croatia walked out of the presidency, because they did not agree with the enforcement of a state of emergency in the country, because no external threat existed to the country. Throughout that time, our doctrine was that the army should prepare itself to defend the country from external aggression and, since no such danger existed, but the intentions were different altogether, the representative of Slovenia did not agree with that proposal of the Federal Secretary and he walked out of the session -- of the meeting. Then another way was sought. The Presidency did not meet on the 13th but on the 14th and the 15th, in order to try and achieve that consensus, one way or another. At that session, again, a decision could not be taken, because there was no consensus. The representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though he was a Serb by ethnicity, and they had counted on him 100 per cent, that he would agree to the introduction of a state of emergency, Bogicevic, the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a participant of those events, has reported in detail how these meetings evolved. In effect, this was an announcement of the future war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, after all those events, was the Yugoslav People's Army used against the republics of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the proposal of the Federal Secretary was not adopted, the Presidency, which was not fully represented at the meeting, it did everything to use the army, allegedly to protect Yugoslavia and to ensure its survival, but that was not what it was -- it was in fact the aim to create a Greater Serbia, so they decided to capture the borders, which they wanted to be the borders of Greater Serbia, so the army was deployed on 25 June, without the Slovenian leadership being informed. The army set its mechanisms in motion under the excuse that it was protecting its borders with Austria and Italy in the north. The Slovenes considered this to be an attack on a regular State which had already been recognised on Slovenia. The deployment of the army in the war in Slovenia lasted for about one month. After that, after the 752 Resolution of the Security Council, the forces were withdrawn from Slovenia. The real reason for the deployment of the army in Slovenia was a calculated move so that, with a fictitious war with no major destruction or casualties, all this was reduced to a minimum, the only thing was to find an excuse for the army among Yugoslav public opinion -- the aim was to withdraw two corps -- the Maribor and Ljubljana Corps -- from Slovenia and while this war lasted, the equipment, the officers, the command structure, the civilians -- they were all withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into the war in Slovenia in detail. Will you please tell us whether, after that, the army was used in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Parallel with the war in Slovenia, combat operations started in Croatia as well. Actually, the Yugoslav People's Army was used in combat in Croatia so that, in the initial stages already, a major massacre was carried out against the population. By way of an example, Vukovar -- the world public opinion is already familiar with the casualties -- they were able to see columns of refugees and the suffering of the Croatian people at the hands of the army, which used all its force and all its state-of-the-art equipment to ensure the borders of a Greater Serbia. The border which would run along the coast to Karlovac, Karlobag, Virovitica -- that was the frontier of the imagined Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, after the events in Slovenia and Croatia, where did the military leadership in Belgrade move the effectives of the Yugoslav People's Army to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first document about that was signed by the Federal Secretary, General Kadijevic, the order being to move from Slovenia the 31st Corps of Maribor and the 14th Ljubljana Corps to Bosnia and Serbia. However, we have information, according to which those two Corps, or, rather, a part of the Ljubljana Corps, was intended to stay in Bosnia, but since the 17th Corps of Tuzla and the 10th Banja Luka Corps had already suffered losses in the fighting in Slavonia, these Corps were mainly used to reinforce the Banja Luka Corps in the fighting in Croatia. A second order envisaged the final withdrawal of forces from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but this happened after the Resolution 572 of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have not yet finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then perhaps you could use the map and show us where the military effectives of the Yugoslav army were moved to, from Croatia and Slovenia to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a pointer and I think there is a pair of headphones with a longer cord that you could use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Sarajevo, this is Banja Luka, Bihac, this is Herzegovina, Mostar, Bileca, Zenica, Tuzla (indicates). In the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, the following forces were withdrawn -- the Rijeka Corps was moved by boat along the Adriatic to Herzegovina and it was actually deployed in Herzegovina. The 31st Corps was moved from Maribor to the areas of Banja Luka, Zenica, Tuzla. Parts of the 14th Ljubljana Corps were transferred to Mrkonjic, Kupres and Sipovo. The 5th Corps was moved from Zagreb to the Bihac district. The educational institutions were moved from Zagreb to Sarajevo, the artillery educational centre and the anti-aircraft defence centre, so that, in effect, four Corps were brought to this territory, and from before we already had in Bosnia the Sarajevo, Tuzla and Banja Luka Corps, so three already existed and four were brought in, which meant seven Corps -- they may not have all been fully manned -- of the Yugoslavia army, not counting the Territorial Defence forces that we shall be coming back to later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in addition to these effectives of the Yugoslavia army coming from Slovenia and Croatia, did other forces come to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have information that, in addition to these Corps of the Yugoslav army, forces came from Serbia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that, a part of the Novi Sad Corps was moved to the region of Bijeljina, a part of the Valjevo Corps to the region of Zvornik , a part of the Uzice Corps to the region of Visegrad and Gorazde, a part of the Podgorica Corps and from Kosovo came to the area of Foca and Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, was not Bosnia totally covered by JNA forces before it proclaimed its independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably there is no precedent of such a great concentration of manpower in such a small area. If we consider the actual numbers of soldiers in this area, there were about 100,000 soldiers, about 800 tanks, about 1,000 armoured personnel carriers, about 4,000 artillery pieces, 100 planes and 50 helicopters, so those were the total effectives covering the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in addition to the Territorial Defence forces, which in Serb parts had organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in 1991, going on to 1992, did the Yugoslav army collaborate with the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the preparations for the war, which was to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to documents and available information, the Yugoslav People's Army was participating in the preparations for the war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those preparations consisted mainly of a distribution of weapons, to citizens of Serb ethnicity. The officers -- army officers were engaged in intensive training of Territorial Defence units and evidence of that is a report of the command of the second military district to the general staff written in March 1992, saying that, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are 69,190 volunteers, which means that already, by then, they had organised unit forming companies, detachment and battalions, that is, 69,000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did the first combat operations begin in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first combat operations started with incidents in 1991 in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac and Bijeljina. I cannot really call them combat, but incidents -- people were ambushed and killed -- so that we immediately took these incidents to be a prelude to provocation for combat operations. As early as 20 October 1991, in the area of Mostar, units of the Yugoslav army appeared without any reason, allegedly to protect the airport. The question was from whom were they protecting it and why were they there? In Mostar, they caused incidents, they looked for excuses in the dissatisfaction of the citizens of Mostar in order to complicate matters. Actually, units of the Yugoslav People's Army that came to Mostar were an introduction to the Dubrovnik operation. It is common knowledge that the Yugoslav People's Army, by its aggression against Croatia, carried out destructive operations in Dubrovnik and the forces that came to Herzegovina were a prelude to the Dubrovnik operation until a resolution of the Security Council was passed, when those operations in the area of Dubrovnik had to be discontinued. I am talking about 1991 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in 1992, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to make a brief introduction. In the course of the fighting, or, rather, when the Yugoslav People's Army came to the territory of Herzegovina, already then intensive fight preparations had begun of volunteers, their training, their arming, their supply with equipment, the formation of units, and in 1992 already, or rather, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, those units were organised to be able to engage in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me, please, when did the Yugoslav general staff take the decision on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav army from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and by what date was that to have been completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Resolution of the Security Council, 752, the general staff took the decision to withdraw forces also from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I cannot recall the date, but that withdrawal -- in any event, there is a document in my expert report from which it can be seen from which garrisons forces were withdrawn to Serbia. However, I wish to say something else. How that withdrawal took place -- perhaps you have another question about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since in your expert report you have indicated that, in mid May 1992, the decision was taken on the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the documents we see that the deadline was 19 May, could you please tell us what was the substance of that decision -- who was supposed to be withdrawn, who was supposed to stay on, and what was supposed to stay on, if you could tell us that in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had an original document from which one can see that such orders were issued, that is, for the army to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina by 19 May. This document says that, first of all, the manpower that does not come from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be withdrawn, which meant that soldiers who were born in Bosnia would stay on in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the officers, and, as for the equipment, the order says, if it cannot be withdrawn, then it should be left behind, whereas the effectives should be transported by plane and it is specified from which airports this should be done. However, it is also well known that that document also stipulated the following: depending on personnel decisions, other people could stay on. It was not explicitly said that all people who were not from Bosnia had to go. It depended on the personnel decisions, from which one could conclude that people who were not Bosnians could also stay behind in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition, it is also well known that soldiers were imported -- people who were doing their military service in the former Yugoslavia in the territory of Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, the principle was that a soldier could not serve in his own town, so that quite a large number of Bosnian citizens were recruited as conscripts to garrisons in Serbia, Macedonia and Montenegro and the order was given that those soldiers should be transferred to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, pursuant to this order, as you have just said, the soldiers and officers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina stayed behind and, also, soldiers and officers who were at that moment in time in the territory of the new Yugoslavia came to Bosnia to continue to do their military service in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me, please, at that time, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there the creation of a military power of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said earlier on that, during 1991, the SDS Party intensively worked towards the organisation of the citizens of the Serb ethnicity to make them an armed force, to turn them into an armed force. The document that -- I mentioned that General Kukanjac sent a document, a report to the head of the general staff which states that, before 20 March, he had in Bosnia 69,190 volunteers, organised volunteers in units, and the document furthermore stipulates that the army armed them, equipped these units, the 50,000-odd of them, that is to say, 70 per cent, whereas the Serbian Party, the SDS Party, armed the rest -- the remaining 17 per cent, which makes up the 69,000 personnel. This shows that the army was included into the process of forming, organising, training and equipping with arms as well as was the SDS Party, they worked hand in hand to create Serbian forces, which might, once the Yugoslav People's Army was withdrawn, make a new military power, a new military force of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you know who was chosen as commander of that army of the Serbian republic -- the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the Republika Srpska army was General Ratko Mladic. He was the former commander of the 9th Corps in Knin. He was transferred to Bosnia, he was promoted to the rank of general and he became the commander there. We have information and facts and figures according to which we know the composition of that general staff of the command there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, within the frameworks of your documents -- of the documents you submitted -- you gave us a diagram of the composition of the army of the Republika Srpska, so would you now put that on the ELMO -- it is to be found in annex 3/5, and could you please clarify what this breakdown that you have made in fact signifies? Brigadier, you can take up the pointer and -- we do not have the chart on our screens as yet. The chart is not on the screen yet. Here we have it. If you show us on the ELMO what took place, we will be able to see on our screens, so would you now take up your pointer and show us what happened on the map itself? You can look at the map and we will know what you are pointing to. What does this chart show? It was composed by you; could you tell us what it represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This chart or diagram represents the distribution of Serb forces after the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army, so that we have the following formations -- the 1st Krajina Corps and this is its responsibility zone; it worked within that zone. Then we have the 2nd Krajina Corps with its headquarters in Banja Luka -- the 2nd Corps has this second zone of responsibility with its command in Drvar. Furthermore, we have the East Bosnian Corps with its headquarters Bijeljina -- the Drina Corps, which was formed a little later on, with its headquarters in Vlasenica. The Srajevo Romanija corps with its headquarters in Lukavica, which is near Sarajevo -- the environs of Sarajevo. Then we have the Herzegovina Corps with headquarters -- it was in Trebinje and then moved on to Belavice, but the main headquarters were in Han Pijesak on Gromanje for the supreme command, in the case of an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you tell me of the forces that the corps had -- what was placed at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first Krajina Corps had in its composition a motorised brigade, the 7th Light Brigade and the 19th Light Brigade. In addition to this, it had special units, mixed artillery battalions, a light brigade, artillery brigade -- the overall force of the 1st Krajina Corps was 55,000 men, 180 tanks, 150 armoured transporters, and 360 artillery pieces. The 2nd Krajina Corps had 14,000 men, 60 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, do you really need all this? At least you know your defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to ask you to tell us what the manpower forces in the Sarajevo and Herzegovina Corps, not to mention the other parts of the republic that did not have any vital effect on what we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Corps in its composition had 12,000 men, 60 tanks, 30 armoured transporters and 200 artillery pieces. The Herzegovina Corps had 22,000 men, 100 tanks, 100 armoured transporters, or APCs, and 260 artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Brigadier, what were the basic characteristics of the combat effectives of the Serbian forces at the beginning -- the initial stages of the war and, in the course of the war, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic characters of the initial operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina were the following: first, the Serbian forces, the Serb forces during peacetime, under so-called "manoeuvres", were placed at dominant positions. All the key points throughout the country -- the cross-roads, the bridges, and what is essential for the defence and so, for example, in Sarajevo, as early on as March 1992, the city of Sarajevo was surrounded by Serb forces -- they had taken up their positions, the artillery, the rocket systems, and, when the citizens asked what was happening, they said that these were regular manoeuvres, and that the army -- this was in the army's plan and that nobody should fear these manoeuvres. Of course, this was all prepared in advance, to have an encirclement around the city of Sarajevo -- it was in fact a blockade of Sarajevo -- and, later on, with the development of events, we were able to see the true purpose of these manoeuvres and of why these particular positions were taken up and manned. On 6 April, there was a serious attack on the city of Sarajevo itself, using the artillery, along all points. Both civilian and other institutions -- departments, hospitals -- the attacks came from all sides and attacked all institutions and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, when Professor Hadzibegovic gave his testimony, we showed the court what happened on that particular date. I should like to ask you to dwell on questions on which you are an expert and can help the court. After this terrible attack on the town of Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after the attack on the proclaimed recognised State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what were the reactions of the legal Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what measures were undertaken to defend the integrity of the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, faced with this kind of danger, the legal Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina undertook the first initial steps to defend the country. First of all, there was a proclamation by which the Territorial Defence headquarters were replaced and a new Territorial Defence headquarters was set up and this was a decree of 8 April. On the same day, a decision was made. The decision was called, "The decree on the threat of war" and on the basis of these decisions, the Defence Ministry and the new headquarters, the new general staff of the Territorial Defence for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, elaborated instructions -- drew up instructions for a reorganisation of the Territorial Defence units, which underwent significant changes with the decree of introducing a new general staff. A new Ministry of Defence was in fact formed on the occasion, it did not previously exist, and it now came under the competency of this Ministry, the Territorial Defence forces, so the Ministry was responsible to the Presidency of the republic for security in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The decree of 8 April, which we have tendered as evidence to the court, did the Ministry of Defence become the supreme command for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it took control with regard to the control and command of Territorial Defence -- the commanding of the units themselves came under the headquarters of the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said that the Defence Minister, in keeping with this decree and together with the commander, brought in instructions -- and, as I say, this has been tendered into evidence in the court -- could you tell us whether these instructions determined the responsibility of the municipal headquarters to the republican staff -- was subordination regulated in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, so that all the headquarters who had declared themselves loyal to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina were organised in this fashion. There were five headquarters, five staff -- not in Mostar, Livno and Gorazde -- whereas the others declared their loyalty, although a part of the Serbs had left their responsibilities and went to -- crossed into the Serbian side, but these other staff headquarters expressed their loyalty to the Ministry and they continued to command their command and to perform their duties. Within the frameworks of these regional headquarters, there were also Territorial Defence headquarters, and they, too, declared their loyalty to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in subordination, they were responsible for their work to the district staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in a situation in which there were no district staff, as you said, in Mostar, Livno and Gorazde, to whom were the municipal staff subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal staff, which was not able to link their subordination to the district -- which were not in function, were directly linked to the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this relationship last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted until the Corps was formed in that particular district -- in that particular territory. That was the case with the 4th Corps, which means that, in November, the 4th Corps was set up in November -- some time in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us what the key problems and difficulties were in this initial stage of building up an army for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic problem was to create an armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as it was. The Territorial Defence had no weapons, it did not have enough officers. The officers were recruited from the Serbs and, as the Territorial Defence was left without these officers, the situation was very complex. It was difficult to organise an armed force -- it had no armaments, no weaponry, that was the basic problem. It did not have the necessary officers and Cadets -- professional men to command the units, and a major problem was because it had no material basis for an army, because the army does not only use equipment, it needs ammunition, it needs communications, it needs workshops, it needs a whole lot of other things -- it needs a quartermaster, and the army was left without all this equipment and without all these effectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, let us now go to the narrower district of Konjic. Using the map once again, can you tell the court which were the basic characteristics of the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Konjic is about 50 kilometres away from Sarajevo. It is on the main road number 17. There is also a railway line which links Sarajevo via Ploce to the sea, to the coast. The size of the municipality of Konjic is 1,100 square kilometres and it is the largest municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are about 43,000 inhabitants according to the 1991 census and in percentages, 54 per cent are Bosniaks, 25 per cent are Croats, and 15 per cent are Serbs of the population -- the remaining 5 per cent were miscellaneous. These are the geographic characteristics of this area, let us look at them. Konjic is situated between the Bitovnja mountain, the Breskovica mountain, Visocica and Prenj -- these are the mountains that surround Konjic -- it is a municipality in a valley surrounded by hills and mountains, with very small -- very few planes, but the municipality is generally in a valley, situated in a valley surrounded by hills and mountains. It is a very difficult area for the use of large-scale forces and armoured forces -- the manoeuvres are difficult around Konjic, because you cannot have an armoured battalion or any large armoured units in that configuration. Along this railway line and the roads, there are many tunnels -- a lot of stone walls, and it is a very difficult area, but it is easy to isolate these areas and passes and to isolate the town itself. The surrounding hills around the town of Konjic are very easy -- it is easy to fire on the town from the surrounding hills -- the Lake Jablanica, on the north-west, cuts off the population, the Croatian and Bosnian population from the centre, so communications do not exist here, because there is a natural barrier in the form of the lake and the inhabitants cannot communicate with the centre, they are cut off. Therefore, this is a very good area for the -- a small group, small units, which would -- so, there is not a great deal of motor vehicles here and so the manoeuvring space is very restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I think that we all have a much clearer picture of the position of the town of Konjic and we will go back to that later on in your testimony. Can you tell me now, Brigadier, whether, according to your investigation, whether you were able to draw conclusions as to whether the Yugoslav People's Army in the previous period, that is to say, 1991 and at the beginning of 1992, before it withdrew and the SDS, did they make preparations for war in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is characteristic for this situation that the Yugoslav People's Army wielded great influence in this area, together with the SDS Party -- in preparing and arming and training the citizens of the Serb ethnicity for the coming combats. At the beginning, with the operation, a battalion -- it was the 1st Battalion of the 2nd Combat Brigade -- was transported to the village of Borci. This is a high area around the Boracko Lake and there was a training centre there, which was where the battalion was located. That formed the nucleus for further information and training of the Serb units of the volunteers who had left the town of Konjic and worked intensively in this area. They were trained, they were armed, and equipped, and they prepared the Serb population, who had left the town of Konjic. In addition to this locality, there was another one -- shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back and ask you some questions as to the armament that took place, but I would now like to ask you, Brigadier, whether the legal authorities in Konjic, and does your research point to that, did the legal authorities in Konjic try to prevent any kind of conflict and to ask the people to return those weapons peaceably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were intensive political negotiations at that time for the return of the equipment and weaponry, and the president of the municipality took part in these negotiations with the Minister, with Petrovic, and there were discussions, but they were -- and one of the conditions was that the Serbs be allowed to leave Konjic, but this was a failure. They returned and they did everything to stop the Serbs leaving the town, whereas the other side knew why the Serbs should leave the town, so that it could be grenaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your research show in this area around Konjic there were cases where the Serb population responded to the call of the legitimate Government not to rise up against its own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, military investigations did show that in one of the villages where the Serbs lived -- where the Serbs were given weaponry, and arms, this is an area which belongs to the Jablanica municipality -- it is outside Konjic, but the SDS armed the Serbs in Jablanica and as Jablanica did not have a majority Serb population, then the Serbs from Konjic saw fit to supply them with arms. However, when the police learnt of this, learnt that the Serbs had received weaponry, it started negotiations for this weaponry to be returned. The entire population, that is to say, the people who had received these arms, understood the situation in a normal fashion and they lay down their arms -- they surrendered them and they were given receipts for the weapons they had turned in and surrendered. None of the Serbs who had acted in this way were ever called to task. So, in addition to all this, they were not taken prisoner or persecuted -- they surrendered their arms and responded to the call from the legal Government.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did your research lead you to conclude when the combat operations started in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The combat operations in Konjic started around 20 April -- I do not recall the exact date -- I think it was 20 April, with an infantry attack on the village of Ljubljana. The attack was repulsed but more serious operations, such as shelling of the town with the help of the air force and the artillery, I think started on 4 May. I am not quite sure about the dates -- I think it is 4 May. That was the beginning of combat operations -- actually it was 20 April, even though there were incidents before that. A citizen from Konjic was wounded, the population was driven out of the surrounding villages -- it was already clear that things were not good -- checkpoints were formed, persecutions started -- all these are indications that combat operations were to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, when you were describing the characteristics of Konjic, you did not tell us whether there were any military facilities in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did not ask me that, but I can tell you that, from the military aspect, from the military standpoint, Konjic was an important strategic target, which the Serbs wanted to keep control of at all costs, because Konjic has a factory of ammunition. It was probably one of the largest in the Balkans, if not the largest -- it manufactured up-to-date ammunition. Secondly, there was a facility in the area for the accommodation of the State and military leadership of Belgrade, which means of Yugoslavia -- it was known as "Ark", or the code was DO. This facility was underground, it was prepared for control and command and even in the event of the use of nuclear weapons. It had complete infrastructure, halls for meetings, debates and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we do not need to go into the details. Were there any other facilities, because if this was for the supreme command, it must have been well equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other facilities where houses, depots, barracks -- let me mention Celebici, which is a barracks close to the M17 road, 50 metres from it. It was a special-purpose depot for army oil reserves and some weapons, but the main purpose was for oil reserves and for troops. Then there was a barracks at Zlatije -- that was a communications centre from which the leadership in Ark could control operations .

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did the legal authorities of Konjic, according to your research and in accordance with the intentions of the new State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to place under its control all facilities in its territory, did the legal authorities of Konjic try, by peaceful means, to take control of the military facilities in its territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the legal authorities asked -- required that those facilities be taken over from the army, particularly the facility Ljuta that I have not mentioned -- it is an arms depot -- this was a depot guarded by the army, and the entire weaponry for three municipalities was housed there -- the municipalities of Konjic, Jablanica and Prozor. Then there was also army weaponry for a brigade which was envisaged as a formation in the region of Konjic -- an army brigade. All the attempts for these facilities to be taken over, negotiations were conducted with Lieutenant-Colonel Velickovic, they went on for a long time -- he made promises, they wanted their own weapons back, but all these negotiations failed. The aim was to gain time, so that the army was not prepared to surrender those weapons, or those facilities, even though those weapons legally belonged to the citizens, or rather the municipalities, because, in the preparatory period prior to the war, all the weapons of the Territorial Defence were purchased with funds out of the budget of the republic and this budget was collected through taxation of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me, after the failed negotiations with representatives of the army, did the legal authorities of Konjic, nevertheless, take over all those facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did. They took over the facilities in the town -- some of them without battle, some with minor operations, without casualties so that, for instance, the Celebici warehouse was captured without resistance by agreement between the head of the guards -- there were about 20 or 30 soldiers there -- and he promised to surrendered it on condition that none of his soldiers were to be killed and that they should be allowed to go and that is how it was taken over, without combat. The soldiers were released home, some of them were from Serbia and they were allowed to leave. Other facilities involved some minor battles. For example, the factory was surrendered without battle, but the facility Ark, and the depot Ljuta, entailed battle on 25 and 26 -- I think -- and, after a short battle, the TO forces, the MUP and the HVO captured these facilities as well as a part of the armaments. However, the air force immediately shelled the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, since you have given a date which differs slightly from the one found in your expert report -- in your report it says that these facilities were taken over between 8 and 12 May. Is this date correct? Was it a slip of the tongue when you said 25th and 26th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I cannot remember all those dates. There are two volumes of documents, so I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you are free to consult your documents -- that is why they are there before you. So I see, that was a slip, an error. So, after these facilities were taken over, which these operations ended on 12 May, did members of the JNA, who had been in Konjic until then, did they all leave the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the last to leave were those from the Zlatije communications centre above Konjic -- after a short battle, according to the data that I have managed to find, they were taken home, taken away by helicopter, and so their presence in the area of Konjic was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So let me go back to the point where I interrupted you a while ago. Will you tell me, the locality of Donje Selo, a local community of the Konjic municipality, did it have any military significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into that a moment ago -- regarding the way Serb inhabitants grouped themselves under the influence of SDS propaganda, they abandoned the town, and rallied in certain areas where they had a majority. One of those was Donje Selo, Bradina, Borci, Zagorice, these were areas in which the Serb population rallied under the influence of the SDS Party propaganda. As for this village of Donje Selo, it is south or south-west of Konjic -- it was an area in which the Serbs blocked the way towards the coast and towards the population on the other side of the lake. They set up a checkpoint there, and prevented communication -- the use of roads -- and the movement of inhabitants towards Konjic. From the military aspect, this meant that the road between Jablanica and Konjic was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleagues are reminding me that you yesterday granted Mr. Landzo permission to see a dentist and this was planned for 11.30. My question is: is it now time for us to adjourn and we can continue with this testimony after the break? If it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will do that. We will adjourn at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Brigadier, will you tell us, please, whether the village of Bradina had any military significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina is a village situated just above Konjic in the direction of Sarajevo on Mount Ivan. This pass is known as Ivan Sedlo. It is very important from the military aspect point of view. If we take into consideration military considerations, offensive operations from the south towards Sarajevo, then this village was very important for the defence of that communication line. Should this feature, this Ivan Sedlo pass fall, it is easier for forces to speed up their advance towards Sarajevo. Therefore, who controls Ivan Sedlo from the direction of Konjic, which means who controls positions south-west of it, that party, by holding those positions, can prevent offensive operations against Sarajevo. Also, in the event of offensive operations from the direction of Sarajevo, again, it is important for preventing penetration of forces towards Konjic. It is also important because whoever controls this pass can shell Konjic from there, because the distance is not large -- it is all within the range of artillery. Furthermore, this pass, there is a tunnel, there are bridges, and they can all be destroyed. So, who controls this area can prevent communication between Konjic and Sarajevo -- by controlling this feature, that is, the village of Bradina, there is no other way to reach Sarajevo, the centre of the republic. The communication line is such that it can be destroyed, whereby obstacles can be formed and thereby Defence improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will reassemble at 2.00pm. (11.30am) (Luncheon adjournment) 23 24 25 (2.00pm) (The witness entered the courtroom)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I go to my next question for the witness, could he be shown the second folder, with the number V2 so that I can continue with my examination? (Handed). Brigadier, before the break, in answer to one of my questions, you said that the Serb population in the local community of Ostrozac had been armed and how they had surrendered those arms. I should like to ask you now to open your folder, chapter IV/4. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this chapter, there is an official report attached by you as well as a list of persons who were illegally armed, and several certificates on objects seized. Brigadier, did you obtain these documents for the means of this testimony and are these the documents on the basis of which you expressed an opinion regarding the arming of this population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this annex of IV/4 shows that this is a list of persons and the public security station of Jablanica seized weapons from these persons, of which they were in possession illegally. They were the inhabitants of the locality of Ostrozac in the Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just asking whether your opinion and what you said about this population was based on the documents that you have enclosed in this folder. Brigadier, in your report, you say that in quite small settlements parts of the Serb population were armed, in chapter IV/3 of this same volume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We find some documents -- as far as I can see, they bear a stamp. Could you tell me the source of these documents, which are mostly hand-written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I obtained this document from the Institute for the Investigation of Crimes. It is hand-written and it comes from a small locality called Glavaticevo, Topalovic Strahinja -- Borislav is addressing Strahinja, the person who was arming the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, you do not have to interpret this document, because it has been enclosed. My question is: was this document one of those that you had collected and on which you relied in your report, saying that the inhabitants of Ostrozac were armed prior to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it can clearly be seen from these documents that there were armed civilians with 10 rifles, and this individual, Topalovic is addressing this other man who was providing the arms, saying that he has 44 able-bodied men who can join in the combat operations and asking him for more weapons. In this connection, from the following document, we can see that he received automatic rifles -- nine such rifles, so Glavaticevo earlier on had 10 rifles and received another nine new ones, which means 19 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break we discussed the importance of the locality of Bradina both in terms of the defence of Sarajevo and the defence of Konjic. In your report, Brigadier, you also say that the population there was armed. Would you please look at your annex IV/9 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This enclosure IV/9 was also verified by the Institute for the Investigation of War Crimes. It is an excerpt from statements by soldiers captured, or rather citizens of Serb ethnicity, who had been captured during combat operations in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you rely on this report among the other documents that you had when expressing your opinion that this population was also illegally armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be seen from this excerpt and from the interrogation of these people, according to their own statements, what kind of arms they had been issued, how many bullets they had been issued, who was the commander, and who gave him the weapons. In more or less all of these cases -- and we can see from their original statements there are 136 men from Bradina, and we see that they were armed, that they were organised, because they talk about their leaders, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, all that can be found in your report. My question was simply whether this was a document that you relied on among others for expressing your opinion. Brigadier, will you please put on the ELMO the table showing the strength of the Serb forces -- I think it is, according to your documents, annexe IV/8, and could you please explain this table for us. As far as I am able to see, you made it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we sharpen this table a little bit? Can we focus on it a little, please? It should be reduced in size -- no -- not so much, please -- a little less -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, very briefly, Brigadier, tell us what does this table show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This table shows a list of Serb forces in the territory of Konjic in the period April/May 1992. In the first column, we have information for parts of the second JNA brigade located in the village of Borci -- total strength about 1,000 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is not necessary, Brigadier, to go into the details but would you tell us in general terms, because we have the data in the table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be seen that, in several locations, there was an army that was armed, Borci, Ljuta, Celebici, Donje Selo, Blaca, Zagorica, Bradina, Borasnica, Teritorija Opstine and Ostrozac and special units totalling 2,516 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can remove the table now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for my delay. I had to have my PC repaired, so I do apologise. I beg for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did your research show that in 1992 parts of the Serb population in the settlement called Bradina blocked the town of Konjic from their side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to the deployment of Serb forces, together with parts of the JNA in the village of Borci, shows that parts of the town of Konjic were encircled. The deployment of forces in Bradina, and further on, to the south and the west, as far as Donje Selo, Serb forces were deployed in such a way that the town was under total blockade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, as you spoke this morning about the shelling of the town from the beginning of May, was this that you have just told us sufficient reason, in military terms, for the situation in Bradina to be dealt with by force of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the conditions that the town of Konjic found itself in, lacking the elementary conditions for normal life, without any contact with the capital of the State, without the possibility of communication with the south, there was no possibility of supplies -- vital supplies to be brought in to the town from the south -- it was necessary, through negotiation, or by force of arms to deal with the problem of the siege of Konjic. Efforts were made to deal with the problem through negotiation with the Serb side and to persuade them to surrender their weapons. However, the case was not the same as in Ostrozac. The forces in this case were far stronger and their task was to prevent at all cost any communication with the centre of the country, that is, with Sarajevo. As those negotiations were unsuccessful, it was normal that the problem should be dealt with by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, will you please tell me, as we have just discussed how part of the Serb population had prepared itself for the war, tell me, did your research show whether a part of the Croat population had also engaged in preparations for the forthcoming events -- in Konjic, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the situation in Croatia where the war was already ongoing, a part of the population of Croat ethnicity in the territory of Konjic municipality was prepared so as not to be caught off guard and the fighters from this area, that is, the soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, participated in the fighting in Croatia. They went under arms to -- and, with the help of Republic of Croatia, Croatian armed forces were organised, so that, in this period, about 750 men of Croatian ethnicity were under arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in view of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina had become an independent State on 6 April, was there a constitutional obligation for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend their country, should it be under threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a constitutional right and duty of all nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the event of war to defend their country, so I wish to underline, "a right and duty".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in that period, that is, in April 1992, did the armed Croatian people, or, rather, the HVO, voice its readiness to carry out its constitutional obligation and to defend the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the initial stages of the war citizens -- Croats -- organised, and better trained and better armed, did participate in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell me how the preparations actually started -- the preparations of the legal authorities in Konjic -- for defence and when did they start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first beginnings of the organisation of the Defence forces of Konjic date back to the last assembly session of the Konjic municipality, which was held on 17 April, when a decision was taken to organise the Territorial Defence, or, rather, a proposal was made to appoint the commander of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did your research provide an answer to the question whether, as early as 17 April -- did that municipal assembly meeting implement the new regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the reorganisation of the Territorial Defence and their subordination to the republican staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as a decree issued by the presidency dated 8 April, reorganised the defence, that is, the old system of Territorial Defence organisation, which was in force until the dissolution of Yugoslavia had to be revised and the Territorial Defence had to be reorganised. A Defence Ministry was set up as part of that reorganisation -- as I have already said -- and below the Defence Ministry was the republican TO staff and then subordinated to that staff were the district staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact, Brigadier, that you said that the district staff in Mostar, to which the Konjic municipal staff should have been normally subordinated did not exist, who was the municipal staff of Konjic subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Konjic municipal staff, in view of the situation in Mostar, was directly accountable to the supreme command in Sarajevo, which means that it was directly subordinate to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, the TO staff and its organisation, as you have indicated in your report, had its own developed structure. I would like to know now, Brigadier, whether you could tell us how the Territorial Defence staff was organised after its reorganisation pursuant to the regulations passed by Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was it a staff with a developed organisational structure as befits staff of this kind? To facilitate your explanation, I would ask you to put under the ELMO the diagram enclosed in your documents and this is in the third volume and I would like to ask it to be given to the witness. (Handed). It is chapter 5/D5. Tell me, please, Brigadier, who made this diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This diagram was done by Midhat Cerovac, who was the chief of staff in the municipal staff throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer my question, linked to this diagram, whether there was a developed organisational structure of the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One can see from this diagram that the staff was established from the very beginning of the war that was similar to what we had before the war, but under changed conditions, and adjusted to the law on the armed forces. We cannot see very well here. May I use it like this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a diagram. It depends on you, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see the letters very well if I place it under the ELMO. Can I use a microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the basis of the foundation of what has been said about this document so far, it is difficult to understand how this witness can speak of the truth of the contents of this document in his evidence, considering it is a document that is said to be or stated to be drawn up by Midhat Cerovac. One would expect Cerovac could come along and tell us about it and we would then know whether what he says is correct or not. Presumably if he drew it up he knows all about it. If this witness says, "This is something I have received and I have relied on it," then I do not object to that, but I do object to it if he is going to assert that what is contained in here is correct, on the basis of what he said so far. All he has told us so far is that this is a document drawn up by somebody else and he appears to be going on to assert the truth of the contents of it. In view of its author, then I object to that, particularly on the basis of the foundation that has been laid so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think Ms. Residovic can reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you know that I have not asked the witness to authenticate the truth of the contents, but, since he has, by relying on this diagram of the municipal staff, expressed his opinion whether this was a developed structure or not, I would like to ask him to be allowed to explain it to us. As for the truth of the contents of this document, we will authenticate it through another witness, but I want the expert witness to be able to use it as he relied upon it in making his expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that case, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually he is not making any claims about it, other than his ability to explain it. I think that is all he is doing. He can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, without entering into whether or not the facts in this table are correct or not, could you explain to the court, as an expert witness, what this diagram represents as regards the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not maintain that this document was a truthful document; I was just told to explain the development and structure of the staff of the headquarters and, therefore, I will try, in that connection, to explain this and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you need not go into those matters. The Defence will decide whether it will call extra witnesses or not. Now, I apologise, I cannot hear the Bosnian translation but the French. I am hearing the French over the earphones. Could that be put right, please? Yes, thank you, that is better. Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure of the staff of the Territorial Defence, from this document, you can see that at the head of the staff of Territorial Defence you have the commander. Under his command, directly under his command, he had the staff, the commanders in charge of morale -- morals -- security, logistics, and the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, are we talking about a highly ramified diagram for the staff or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document, we are able to conclude that this is a well developed staff, that it was able to perform all its functions, starting out from the commander -- the chief of staff. The chief of staff has an assistant for operative and educational tasks and he is the deputy chief of staff at the same time. Then we have the intelligence branch. Then we have operative and educational tasks once again -- training -- and officers. Then we have a service or branch for organisational and mobilisational purposes, an informative and computer centre, and the different branches of the army. We have the head of the artillery and his subordinates, the head of the engineering department and his subordinates, we have the engineers, the artillery and the armoured units, the anti-aircraft units, air force and air defence units and the communications unit, so that is more or less the structure which comes under the chief of staff. The morale department body have their own offices and we have offices for information and propaganda activities. The security body also has its offices. The logistics department body has a backbone with the different services, which, on the basis of logistics, determined combat effectiveness, so let us take that in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not think we need to go into all these details, as we have the chart in front of us -- you have given us enough information so far, and you did say that it was a highly ramified staff with all its members, and was it the head of some combat units -- did it stand at the head of combat units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal staff and the commander in chief, he was the commander in chief -- the commander in chief was the supreme organ and he was in charge of issuing commands, so it is only the commander in chief and the commanders who had the right to make decisions on the use of the different units within the staff and they were there to command those units. Everybody else, regardless of their function within this staff, did not have the right to command. They did not enjoy the right of command; it was only the commander in chief and the deputy commander who had the right and duty to do so, and to see to the stated use of these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, may I interrupt you? We shall be going back to the question of command later on. I apologise, but let us look at the structure of the staff after the session of 17 April. In your document or report, under V-D/4 you give a list of the members of that staff. May we take a look at that list under V-D/4? Would it be correct to say, Brigadier, that this contribution -- this list -- was drawn up by the head of the municipal staff at the time, Midhat Cerovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you received this list from Mr. Cerovac and that you relied on this when you gave your expert opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, from the research you performed, as you said, on the spot in the localities and via your documents, could you tell us what the organisation of the Territorial Defence of Konjic was like on the spot -- on the locality -- what did it look like, that is, during 1992 from the onset of 1992 -- on the ground, what did the Konjic Territorial Defence in actual fact look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To begin with, Territorial Defence of Konjic consisted of parts of the Territorial Defence of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, and the police. For some time, the HOS forces were active, too, but these were symbolic -- there were very few members of HOS, but these were the basic three structures which made up the defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Brigadier, now, if I may, to answer my next questions by first looking at the diagram of the overall defence force, which, in your annex, V-D/2, you submitted in your documents. V-D/2, that is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is an error here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: D/2 or D-2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a list of active military personnel engaged in the work at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, the defence forces of Konjic, that is a different document. Maybe I have the wrong numbers. Let me check that. Perhaps it was V-D/5 -- that is the document I have in mind, because it was Xeroxed again, so I apologise for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, D/5 is the structure of the municipal staff, which I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we leave that for the moment? I am going to ask you some more questions and then, during the break, I will go and check those numbers. Have you found the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is V-D/8, the defence forces of Konjic, a review of the organisation of the defence of Konjic. Here we have a ratio of forces, on the one I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, there seems to be a mix-up there. So, may I ask you to proceed? I would like to ask you some more questions and then, after the break, we will go back, once this matter of numbers and documents has been clarified. Tell me, please, Brigadier, in view of the fact that you have just spoken of the overall forces of the Konjic defence, whether the system of subordination for all these forces of the defence of Konjic was uniform -- was it a uniform system of subordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, there was a specific feature, which, in the system of a command was not known, and that is that we had three structures, and each of the three structures were subordinated vertically from top to bottom. So, for example, the Territorial Defence staff was directly under the command of the supreme command, the commander in chief, in Sarajevo. The HVO or Croatian Defence Council was subordinated to the Grude headquarters, the police was subordinated to its Ministry of Internal Affairs in Sarajevo, and each of these three structures received its orders from its superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your research show, Brigadier, that there was a basis for you to come here to this court today and testify and say whether there were endeavours for the defence forces of Konjic to make them more compact in view of the fact that they had the same defence goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. This was done immediately, so that these three structures could work in a way -- as a single body in the combat operations and that is why an attempt was made to form a body, which would unify the planning and use of those forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, Brigadier, you state that, on 12 May, that certain joint bodies were formed. Could you tell us about those bodies -- what were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of previous agreements and in view of the existing situation in Konjic, in the aim of using the defence forces as effectively and efficiently as possible towards the town's defence, an agreement was made to set up, to form a joint command, which would be composed of the Territorial Defence forces, which were later called the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Brigadier, was the formation of this joint command of Territorial Defence and the Croatian Defence Council, was it foreseen by the rules or was it an expression of their defence activities and the way they worked together, or was it on the basis of a set of regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this was a specific situation for Konjic itself, because it was not the usual kind of plan and diagram in the system of command and control. It is possible that a similar system existed in certain other parts and that the problem was similar elsewhere, that is to say, that a compromise had to be sought and found in view of subordination, because the forces of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, never fulfilled their orders coming from the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas, in that respect, the police showed greater solidarity and did perform its decisions -- acted on its decisions, so this is a specific feature which was an expression of prevailing conditions, so that the forces were to be used as effectively as possible to defend the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, let us verify, first, whether, in annex V-D/10, whether that is the diagram, the chart for the joint command, and, if it is, then I would like to go on and ask you several questions. Is this chart -- was this chart drawn up by Midhat Cerovac, who was the commander of the staff of Konjic's Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was also a chart which was drawn up by the chief of staff, Mr. Midhat Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you, in addition to the other documents in drawing up your report, did you rely on that chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Do you want me to explain the chart?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am going to ask you questions and we will do it that way. Tell me, please, who, according to your investigations, was the chief of staff for the joint command -- the commander for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The function of the commander of the joint staff was the commander of the municipal staff of Konjic, Mr. Ramic Esad -- Esad Ramic and as he was ill Boric Omer was his deputy, and the chief of staff was a Croat, he was in this particular case Zebic, Dinko Zebic. All the other bodies were mixed body, but it is essential to note one particular fact here, and that is why do we call it the "joint staff" -- "joint command". They harmonised, they dovetailed their decisions, they decided together on the use of the forces. Without both signatures, nothing could be done, so they had to have both signatures for operations to take place. The commander of the joint staff issued commands to the Territorial Defence units, whereas the head of staff, Zebic, would issue commands to his own units.
