utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did this mean, in practice, that the joint command had two equal commanders -- commanders of equal footing, of equal standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that is a unique example. As I said, this was through force of necessity -- conditions necessitated this in order to use the forces as effectively and efficiently as possible, but, in military theory and practice, no such similar example has been heard of, because, in the system of command and control, there is always one sole commander -- that is the basic principle -- one superior, one commander, who makes the decisions, and who then is responsible for the use of his units. This was an exception, as I say, and so, in this case, and for everything that took place within the Territorial Defence units, it would have been the commander of the municipal staff, whereas everything that took place with the HVO units, the commander there would be the chief of staff in the joint command -- in the joint staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, were these two commanders equal -- commanders of an equal standing, as you called them, did they sign all the commands issued together -- the ones they had decided on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at the many documents that I had before me, I saw the signatures -- both signatures. However, without both signatures, the document would not be fully in force -- valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When this joint staff functioned, were the nominations signed by both commanders, that is, the Territorial Defence and the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they both signed the nominations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell me, please, in view of the war situation in May and June of 1992, whether, in the defence sense, this function of joint command, did it give off certain results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because the results of the initial operations, where they acted together, where the Territorial Defence forces and the Croatian Defence Council's forces acted jointly, better results were achieved, because they joined forces, which meant that they were not only numerically stronger, but the command was stronger and more successful -- control and command and coordination between the two forces went via the joint staff, the joint command, so that the forces knew their zones of activity, their concrete tasks at that particular stage and the goals they were to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. You said at the beginning that the HVO and part of the Croatian people organised within the Croatian Defence Council had a certain amount of legitimacy, because they were ready and willing to defend their State, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me now, please, Brigadier, whether, later on, with the adoption of new regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO became part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the enactment of the law on armed forces in May 1992, the armed forces were made up of the Territorial Defence units and the BiH Army, and the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to the questions we mentioned earlier on in connection with Konjic. Could you tell me, please, regardless of the joint goals and interests which they had in the country's defence, whether the joint command, during 1992, ceased to function in actual practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to developments in Konjic, and according to my own research, I was able to see that the joint command functioned successfully, especially in parts where the location had to be cleared up in Donje Selo, but when the Operation Oganj was resorted to, although they worked jointly to plan this operation, Operation Oganj, before the actual commencement of the attack, before the attack was actually launched, the representative of the HVO, the head of chief of staff, said he was not going to take part in the execution of that particular Operation, and I would like to stress here what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we go on to this explanation, I should like to ask you first to look at your document, V-D/11 -- is that the order in question, which was signed by the commander Omer Boric and Dinko Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the documents on the basis of which you present your views here in court and your opinions of how the orders were issued in the joint staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document you can see that they were co-signatories, Commander Zebic and Omer Boric signed the document jointly and they were authorised to do so, to sign this joint document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you check this document in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, or in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Konjic. I did in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now, Brigadier, take a look at your contribution V-D/12. Is that, Brigadier, an example of a nomination signed by the commanders of the HVO and the joint staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an authorisation, not a nomination. It authorises Goran Lokas, for purposes of the HVO and the municipality of Konjic, to perform security work, and it was signed by Dinko Zebic of the HVO and Boric, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether this is one of the documents on which you base your assessments that authorisations and other acts in the joint staff were signed jointly by the two commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said earlier on that none of the documents which were not signed by both the commanders would hold water, so both signatures were needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you were just about to explain the virtual discontinuation of the functioning of the joint command, even though those forces continued to engage in defensive activities. Could you tell me, what did your research show as to why this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my view that the Croatian forces did not receive permission from Grude, because they had planned the joint operation until the very last moment, and this could be linked to politics, because the Croatian Defence Council had its own interests and aims regarding the territories that they proclaimed to be Croatian, or, rather in the Croatian interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in order to avoid further elaboration of that thesis, let me ask: if a joint operation had been engaged in, in the direction of Borci, would that order have had to have been signed by both commanders, that is, both the TO commander and the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Brigadier, to look at V-D/15. Is this an order dated 27 May, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether this is a supplementary order for the battle in Bradina, and is it visible from this very text that such an order had to be signed by the commander of the TO and of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find this order in the archives of the BiH Army, or, rather of the army in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is an order that has already been admitted into evidence by this Trial Chamber, but I just wanted to know whether you had verified its authenticity. Brigadier, which assumptions did you use, or, rather, were there any military orders for the defence forces of Konjic to undertake the liberation of temporarily occupied areas in the south eastern part of Konjic near the Boracko Lake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document of the supreme command instructing an offensive to liberate the areas of Konjic via Borac, Nevesinje and Kalnovik -- there is such an order issued by the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we examine your annex, D/24 in the same volume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you verify this document in the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I found it in the supreme commander archives, or, rather the general staff now. This document exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Croatian Defence Council, at the time, was under the law a part of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it also obligatory and binding on the units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, the Croatian Defence Council could receive orders according to the chain of command only from Grude, because the top leadership of the two forces was not united. Each of these forces were separate. There was not a body that would unite these two headquarters -- in Grude and in Sarajevo. So, this order could be binding on the municipal staff -- it is addressed to the municipal staff -- and, as this was not in the interests of the Croatian Defence Council, because Nevesinje and the entire area of western Herzegovina was not in the sphere of interest of the Croatian Defence Council and that is why they did not wish to engage in battle in those areas, even though they all belonged to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that actually mean that somewhere around this time the Croatian Defence Council, in practice, began to obstruct certain activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already, as early as the end of June, by cancelling its participation in the Operation Oganj, the HVO began its obstruction, even though they continued to constitute part of the defence forces of Konjic. Until the Corps was formed they held on to their positions, they had control of the defence lines, they sought in the town of Konjic to organise their own authority -- in a sense to appoint their own people to executive posts in the economy -- there is a document to that effect, but, in any event, they discontinued to engage in conflict with the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can we now look at your annex D/25? Is it a document dated 25 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you verify this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the archives of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the archives of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a military expert, would you say that this document is a description of preparatory activities by the municipal staff and the HVO before the beginning of the Operation, which they were ordered to engage in on 20 June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the municipal TO staff has addressed this document to the HVO staff in Konjic. The subject is, "Coordination of Combat Operations within the Territory of Konjic Municipality" and this is a document linked to the order to the command of the municipal staff of Konjic to prepare an operation against Borci, Nevesinje and Kalinovik. That is the document. The commander of the TO staff proposes to the HVO how far they should go, and where they should fight, so, in a sense, this is the proposal of the commander planning an operation against Borci using joint forces and this was a document from the period when the first signs were evident that they were reluctant and unwilling to participate in the Operation Oganj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can it be seen from this document that the municipal staff, in its preparations for this operation, which according to this document was called Operation Oganj, or "fire", did the municipal staff specify the lines of action, the Tactical Groups for individual directions of combat, while at the same time determining an operative officer, Mr. Cerovac, as the person who was supposed to coordinate these activities. Could you please elaborate on this from the military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal staff here elaborated a plan from which we can see that it is requiring the Croatian defence forces to keep control of a particular area, and to take action in another direction. I do not have the maps to show you all this. Then, it also says that the rest of the forces in this Operation Oganj would form Tactical Groups and each of those Tactical Groups had its own direction of action and the staff is asked to respond to this proposal of the municipal staff and, if they have any counter proposals, to make them, or, if they have any objections, that they should be made, after which they should meet again to discuss the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you adduce from this document who was the commander of Operation Oganj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be seen from this that the commander of Operation Oganj was the commander of the municipal staff, Captain Esad Ramic. He planned the operation and was in command of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Brigadier, that we move on to another subject which you have discussed in your expert report. Could you please tell us, Brigadier, after the municipal assembly meeting of 17 April, did the municipal assembly have the necessary conditions for continuing to work regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the war had already started, the municipal assembly was unable to meet normally and, in accordance with the regulations of the republic, it set up a presidency, which had all the jurisdiction of the assembly, and its obligation was, when the necessary conditions set in, to convene a meeting of the assembly, and to verify the decisions taken in the meantime, but, in any event, it was the presidency who had the authority to take all decisions in the name of the assembly, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your considerable professional and personal experience from the past period, could you please tell us whether the regulations of the former SFRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina, prior to the adoption of new regulations in April 1992, in the case of a state of emergency, was a body envisaged for such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the former Yugoslavia, there was a crisis staff. This will take a little time for me to elaborate, if I may, because it may remind -- be reminiscent of something else. We have to go back to 1972, when a group of saboteurs, of extremist Ustashe forces trained and prepared outside the forces of Yugoslavia. There were 22 men in all in that group, if I recall well, who were fully armed, they were elite troops who were trained for a long time and they were infiltrated into Yugoslavia via Slovenia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where, because it was a wooded and mountainous country, they thought it would be a suitable place for starting an uprising.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Brigadier, the reason was the infiltration of this group from abroad. What then happened with the regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having acquired such experiences, as there were no plans for such contingencies, we only had a war plan that is set in motion in the event of an external aggression. However, this situation made it necessary to elaborate fresh plans for action in such contingencies and these bodies were named crisis staffs and each municipality had such a plan of action for emergencies. This was necessary, because, under such conditions, it was essential to act very expeditiously and to take all steps for such a group to be liquidated as soon as possible, or, in the event of any other such contingency, but in any event, there were forces and a crisis staff that had to deal with the crisis that occurred so suddenly and this was in force until the dissolution of Yugoslavia. With the new regulations covering the field of defence, the law and the armed forces, the law and defence, such laws did not make provision for such crisis staffs, nor do they exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Your Honours, since I do indeed appreciate the excellent presentation of the Brigadier, and, also, in view of his age --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do not mention my age please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, mine then, because I am standing, you see, all the time, so I would ask you, if possible, if we could have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. I think we can break now and come back at 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (3.30pm) (A short break) (4.00pm) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like, your Honours, to take my witness back to the chart that was in question a moment ago, Brigadier. It was your contribution V-D/2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the chart, this review of the organisation of the defence units of Konjic from April to October in 1992 was composed by the chief of staff at the time, Mr. Midhat Cerovac. Brigadier, did you base your opinions on this chart -- were your assessments based on that chart, in your expert report, of course, taking into account all the other documents and your own experience in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you tell us briefly what the chart in fact represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a review of the organisation of the defence forces of Konjic. The Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is subordinated, according to the Territorial Defence staff, that is the line of command, and from that we can see that the Territorial Defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina commands directly the municipal staff of Konjic, and from thence we go further down the line, and the Territorial Defence staff of Konjic and its commander has, under him, his subordinates -- they are the following units, combat units. You can see the combat units there -- Konjic 1, Konjic 2, the Zebcanik Unit, the Gracanica Unit -- it is a bit faded there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we see all that on the chart. Let us go to the second structure, the HVO Croatian Defence Council structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the lines of subordination, we see that the Croatian Defence Council and the Grude HQ has the Croatian Defence Council of Konjic under it, and the Croatian Defence Council then has the HVO units further subordinated. Then the third structure was the police, and we can see that the republican Internal Affairs Ministry is directly superior to the public security service of Konjic, and the public security service has, under it, the police forces, and the structure is as follows: the commander of the municipal staff with dotted line cooperates with the public security service on the left, and on the right, once again, the dotted line, and its relationship towards the HVO -- the Croatian Defence Council. These are the lines of cooperation, and not command -- lines of cooperation along the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. May we now have a look at the chart that you yourself drew up, and it is to be found under V-D/8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please briefly explain what this chart signifies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This chart, once again, depicts the defence forces of Konjic and the relationships that exist, so let us go from the top -- the municipality of Konjic at the top, and the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic, then from the dotted lines we can see that it cooperates with the joint command, so the dotted line of the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic shows that the joint command of the Territorial Defence of the HVO of Konjic is not subordinate to the presidency, but merely cooperates with it. Second, the Ministry of Defence is at the top and under that we have the staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it commands the staff -- the full lines indicate subordination and the dotted line is the line of cooperation. The Internal Affairs Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we look at the straight line, full line, it shows that we have the public security service, to which it is -- which is subordinate and then cooperation with the presidency of the municipality of Konjic. Then we come to the joint command. The war presidency of the municipality of Konjic, with the dotted line indicates that it is not subordinated to the joint command of the TO and HVO -- the joint command is shown here and is shown as commander of the TO, he is commander of the joint staff and on the right-hand side the HVO commander, and, at the bottom, with the joint command, we have the organs of the staff of the joint command -- we already explained that a moment ago and, under the ministry, the Croatian Defence Council, we see that there is the HQ of Konjic and this is a direct line from Grude, and then, at the bottom, the HVO Konjic units, which shows that the chief of staff commands the HQ of Konjic, and the command goes downwards -- the commander of the municipal defence of Konjic with a straight line goes down to Konjic, and the units there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have now shown us the line of cooperation from the presidency to the defence forces. Would you now tell us of the lines of cooperation towards the defence units and what they are composed of? Let me phrase that another way. What rights and responsibilities does the war presidency have towards the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the law, the war presidency of the municipality is responsible for the preparation of the units of Territorial Defence and its forces in the municipality -- it is responsible for their organisation, for equipping them, and for everything else that comes under the sphere of logistics for combat operations. From the chart you can see that the war presidency is not authorised to command the units. That is under the competency of the republican staff -- defence staff. Then we have other complex problems, because the war presidency of the municipality, in addition to the support given to the defence forces, has a lot of work to do with regard to the management of the municipality itself and its organs to supply the population, to organise military production -- wartime production, to organise Civilian Defence and to save the population -- protect the population and all the problems that are not directly linked to the war, and command -- there is no exclusive responsibility on the part of the war presidency. Therefore, the war presidency has other -- deals with other affairs -- not the command of the units and the use of units. Those are not rights which the war presidency enjoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I should now like to ask you to answer the following question: in May -- and you write this in your report -- was there a joint session, a joint meeting, of the military command and the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic -- did they hold a joint meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Conclusions of this kind exist, but tell me the annex -- remind me of the annex so that I can recall the responsibilities of the presidency towards the defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in your review -- in your report, the conclusions that you are talking about now can be found in annex V-A/7. It is in the second volume -- not the one you have before you, but volume number 2 -- dossier number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the number you mentioned -- V?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is A/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, V-A/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is annex IV.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think you will find it at the end -- V-A at the end of volume 2. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the number again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found it now -- I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said, Brigadier, that those were the conclusions from the joint meeting held between the war presidency and the command of the forces. Tell me, please, whether you relied on that document when you made your assessments and whether, in keeping with the other documents, you based your expertise and what you are saying here today on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that document exists and that is why I based my conclusions on it as a true document, and I present my views in my expert report. Part of the conclusions refer to the defence forces. I would like to dwell on that for a moment. The document speaks of the civilian sector and the tasks in that regard, and as it was a joint meeting, a joint session with the defence forces, they were charged with the following tasks: the report of the staff was adopted as to the situation with regard to preparations and the problems that exist, and it was stated that the bodies should be informed of the situation on the spot; that the war presidency must have information from the locality itself -- up-to-date information, because if the war presidency does not know the actual situation, it can take measures which would be inappropriate, to send its organs to territories which are not under the control of the army and that is why they require up-to-date information and reporting on the situation in the locality where there is the danger of an enemy breakthrough, whether the population should be taken to safety. So, this system of reporting and information, in order to inform the civilian population of the defence on the given territory -- there were other important matters, do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you some questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, briefly --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do these conclusions precisely define the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the defence forces of Konjic are the forces I mentioned earlier on -- Territorial Defence of the HVO and the police, and this document determines certain measures to be undertaken. The document testifies to an organisation which requires organisation of the armed forces, and that the regulations and rules of the military police be adhered to and all soldiers not included into the defence structures should be placed within the system so that there is no voluntariness on the part of these soldiers or other individuals. The defence forces of Konjic, the HVO and the police must have the necessary insignia so that can be recognised as representatives -- that their uniforms should have insignia, and commanders of units, so this document is a preparation -- a basis for the army's organisation, so that the army takes on the form of an organised force without any self-appointed units or commanders. So, it is an act, a document, which requires a modern organisation for the army -- organisation based on modern principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of the fact that this document determines the existing fact that the defence forces of Konjic are the HVO, the TO and the police, is it correct to say that, on 18 May 1992, the most responsible subjects of Konjic, that is to say, the war presidency and the military staff, determined that accounts must be settled with any individuals who might be carrying arms in an unorganised fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. This was a document to prevent all voluntariness on the part of individuals, that everything must be organised and within a system, that there are no separate units or commanders with any responsibilities, and to prevent crimes, voluntary action and so on, so this is an act on the organisation -- a document specifying the organisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do these conclusion -- on the basis of these conclusions, do all the authorities in Konjic call for the rule of law on the part of all the authorities and individuals concerned and no arbitrariness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the first part of the document which relates to the civilian sector. These are the tasks for all the structures of power and authority at the municipal level, stipulating how they are to function -- the economic unit and everything else within the area of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does your research show that, after this meeting, the military organs took certain steps within their competence and that the war presidency, on the other hand, took steps within the frameworks of its competencies to put these conclusions into practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war organs saw to the restructuring of the units, and that everything that is stipulated in the document be translated into practice with regard to the defence forces; that the tasks stipulated by the presidency should be fulfilled under given conditions. It was not always possible in a short space of time to deal with all those matters such as uniforms, insignia and so forth, but the process was started, and this type of organisation was unleashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Brigadier, to look at another document V-A/9, by which a committee for funerals is set up, which is evidence in this case. Is this an example that the war presidency immediately began the execution of tasks, which were stipulated for the war presidency as a civilian body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not refer to the tasks relating to the civilian sector, but one proof of this is the stipulation of a commission for funerals in the following composition and it is the task -- this document provides for the commission's work and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that, in what you have said so far, you indicated the many difficulties facing the defence forces and the war presidency, and that you stressed that the supply question was an important one, that is, from the supply of arms to the supply of food, that this was a major problem, is it true, Brigadier -- would you tell me, please, Brigadier, whether your research showed that the defence forces and the war presidency at that time tried, in different ways, to solve the problem of supplies and of overall logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was an important problem for the Konjic region, as was the problem for Bosnia as a whole and that was the logistics problem and I stressed earlier on that Territorial Defence was without arms, without uniforms, without communications, without sufficient food supplies, whereas it had to take on the tasks of Defence, so these were very complex conditions and the greatest problem occurred in the sphere of logistics. There were not enough weaponry, not enough communications, and uniforms, and everything else necessary for waging a war, and satisfying the needs of the commanding units and the needs of the soldiers themselves and we had to find a way out of this, a way of solving the problem, so that we had to transcend the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in your report, and document V-A/21, A/22, A/23, A/24, and concluding with A/24, you propose a series of documents under the title of "authorisations". Would you look at these documents now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several documents which testify to how the war presidency of Konjic endeavoured to solve the problems that stood before it and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Brigadier, did you verify the authenticity of these documents in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was verified in the archives in the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now what these documents represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These documents mostly represent permissions and authorisations granting permission for travel or envisaging resources for supplies and there are quite a number of these documents signed jointly by the joint command and the president of the presidency. These are various permits and authorisations having to do with the procurement of supplies for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of the conditions and circumstances under which the defence in Konjic took place, was it normal for people to receive such permits so that the war presidency could fulfil its tasks as stipulated by law? Was this something typical of the times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were specific circumstances under which the war presidency was operating. Without such permits, it would not be possible to pass through Herceg-Bosna or through the territory of the Republic of Croatia from which mostly this logistical support was provided. Therefore, any officer who had such an authorisation was able to travel through Herceg-Bosna to Croatia, on which we relied for logistic support for the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, since you are familiar with the situation in the whole republic, if I may say so, because your personal experience and research covered that whole area and, in this particular case, you focused on the municipality of Konjic, my question is whether the problem of logistic support and supplies was a major problem for the defence of the whole republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already pointed out that the greatest problem of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the problem of supply with materiel, weaponry, ammunition, medical supplies, communications resources, so that, without production of the same, which did not exist in Bosnia, even though factories did exist, like the one in Konjic, for example, there were no manufacturing components and raw materials for our own manufacturing facilities, so these had to be procured from other places, via the Republic of Croatia. This applied to the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The authorisations, permits, special permits and the like, which were issued to people for them to be able to engage in such procurement in order to mitigate this problem, did these authorisations give the people to whom they were issued any command authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These documents do not have the validity of an order. These are not documents that can be equated with orders. These are authorisations issued in the name of a particular person permitting him to obtain, for the needs, in this case of the municipality of Konjic, certain supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Brigadier, whether, while preparing yourself for this testimony, did you see a decision of the war presidency dated 18 May 1992, whereby Mr. Zejnil Delalic was appointed coordinator between the war presidency and the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that decision. It is a document that has also been verified. The decision was issued on 18 May whereby the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic appoints as coordinator of the defence forces of the municipality of Konjic Mr. Zejnil Delalic. The coordinator of defence forces will directly coordinate work between the defence forces of the Konjic municipality and the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you have that document before you, which is a document that has been admitted into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, Brigadier, whether this decision, in your opinion, was passed by a civilian or a military body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, does such a decision come under the competencies of that civilian body in defence preparations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is something a civilian body could issue, because the decision does not relate to any kind of control or command function in the armed forces. It is purely a question of coordinating activities between the armed forces and the civilian bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please tell me whether this coordinator, as appointed by the presidency, on the basis of your expertise and your experience as a professional officer, does this person have any command or control functions as a military commander or a person in superior authority in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must elaborate in answering this question. In the armed forces, there is no such concept of a coordinator in any formations. If we look at the platoon company, regiment, division, et cetera, there are no persons who are appointed to a post that would be called a "coordinator". All the other posts are regulated -- commander, assistant commander for this and that, the staff consists of such and such -- there is no such concept of a coordinator in the armed forces. There is another expression and that is the expression "coordination". "Coordination" is a function within the system of control and command and it implies coordination of effort of all participants engaged on a common task, so if there are several factors participating in dealing with a particular problem, then this concept of coordination comes into play, implying that all the participants should focus on a particular task so that that task may be achieved with a minimum of losses. In military literature, to be more specific in a text book on control and command, this is in our language called "sadejstvo" or "coordination". This is just a definition. To make myself clearer, I would like to try and show this visually to indicate what that "coordination" implies, or "sadejstvo" as the military term is in our language. If I may be permitted, may I try and illustrate this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you do that, Brigadier, could you tell us whether we are talking about the coordination of combat units, or of other factors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This coordination applies exclusively to combat operations -- "coordination" is a concept in combat, and there is no particular individual who performs that coordination. It is the most senior commander in his zone of responsibility. When a commander implements a decision, or when he conveys it to his subordinates, when he gives them specific tasks or assignments, "The first battalion must do this and the other one that," and so on, in that period of time this most senior commander performs coordination, so that each of these participants knows by way of an example. By way of an example, a brigade has the task of eliminating a battalion in defence. The attack is carried out by the brigade against the battalion. The forces in that regiment consist of various branches, infantry, artillery, communications, et cetera. In this organisation of coordination, when giving them assignments -- let us take as an example in the case of an offensive, the artillery preparation of the attack shall last 30 minutes, the attack shall start at 0600 hours. Therefore, this commander of the infantry battalion, the commander of the artillery unit, the head of the engineers and all the other participants must know that the attack will start at 0600 hours; that the artillery or the fire preparation for that offensive will last 30 minutes to neutralise the enemy defences. In the meantime, the infantry must reach the line of the security zone, so the infantry must reach that particular line, which is 150 or 200 metres removed from the enemy positions -- this is the security zone -- so the infantry should not suffer casualties from the artillery fire. It must not stay there long. Through coordination, the infantry is told to start the assault at such and such an hour. The artillery would cease-fire at 0630 hours. At 0630 the infantry will start its assault. The tanking units are somewhere in the rear. The tanks are primarily to support the infantry in the case of an offensive. They lead the infantry -- they may be two or three kilometres removed from that line. The commander of the tank unit must calculate exactly how long he will need to reach this assault position and, as soon as the artillery transfers the fire into the rear, he must start with his march forward. Therefore all the participants in such an operation must know exactly what their assignments are in terms of time, because otherwise there will be losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I think you have described very vividly to all of us this coordination of military forces. May I ask you now whether, as you just said, that means that coordination in battle is done by the military commander, that is, the person with a senior military position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This coordination or "sadejstvo" is the exclusive task of the commander, who, after a decision has been taken, goes on the ground with his other commanders -- this is not done in offices, this is on the ground. When this coordination is organised, there is no other person who could organise it -- or control or command it -- there is no special body to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, having told us all that, can you answer the following question: can such a coordination be carried out at all by a civilian entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need to ask such a question. A civilian entity cannot interfere in military affairs. A civilian body cannot have any role in the army in terms of the organisation of combat and control and command -- that is out of the question. For that purpose, we have commanders, senior officers, leaders whose exclusive responsibility is the result of the battle and no civilian bodies can issue commands or orders in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the decision of the war presidency on the appointment of Mr. Zejnil Delalic as coordinator. This coordinator, who is there to coordinate between the civilian and military bodies, does he have anything to do with this coordination known to military science and military practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In this particular case, when we are referring to this decision, this coordinator needs to coordinate not with combat units, combat forces -- maybe this is a misuse of terms -- perhaps it is not the best term to be used -- this term is not a good one. The municipality appointed this coordinator to assist the presidency. He is in the service of the presidency -- of a civilian body and he has to ensure logistic support. He has a logistic role, to assist the presidency, which is also responsible for logistic support of the army. Therefore, his function is to assist the army, to convey the needs to the presidency, the needs in terms of logistic support for each operation and to deal with all logistic problems, and not to influence the way in which battles are organised, to plan the battles, because, after all, in this particular case, in this particular individual, I think the only way we can understand it as a function in the service of the war presidency and the war presidency has no authority to impose commanders who have command and control responsibility. That is not the jurisdiction of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. As you have obviously studied in detail, in some detail, the things that happened in Konjic, could you please tell me whether this complicated situation required this coordination and cooperation in other areas, too, and did you come across certain documents in which mention was again made of the coordinator and coordination? Looking through your documentation, I saw documents marked V-A/18. Shall we please examine that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What document did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is such a document on the use of communications in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you verify this document in the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The army archives? Is this one of the documents that you relied upon when you said that, in other areas, too, the need arose for coordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, the use of communications in wartime and this document was jointly signed by the joint staff, by the commanders Zebic and Ramic and another person, Delic, I think. It deals with the need to organise communication. This is also a kind of coordination in the area of communications. There was also an economic staff. They called it a staff, but its role was also to coordinate things in the economy. That applied to all these bodies appointed by the municipality for civilian matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I should now like to ask you, in this third volume of your documents, in annex IX/9, if we could look at a document from that period. Before I proceed with questions about this document, I should like to ask you, Brigadier, whether you could tell us, within the system of control and command in the army, who is the person who commands -- who is the person who issues orders and bears responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first principle in the system of control and command is that there must be one commander. This means that one person must issue the order -- the commander for lower units we call them commandeers and from battalion and upwards they are called commanders. Therefore, the commander is authorised to command -- to control -- and he is -- he suffers all the consequences of his decisions. He may transfer a part of his competencies and powers to his associates, but he cannot transfer responsibility for the situation and the results. Therefore, if he does transfer certain powers to his associates, should anything happen, it is the commander who is responsible. For instance, we cannot allow two people to be responsible for a regiment. It must always be the regiment commander -- even though the chief of staff may have given some orders, in the areas for which he was authorised by the commander, but the responsibility still falls on the commander. That is quite clearly stated in the system of control and command as regards who is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this order, or let me ask you, first, whether you found it in the army archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The one we were looking at -- IX/9, dated 3 June. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: IX/9? This is the one I was talking about. It has to do with the establishment of railway communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you check this order, too, in the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could you comment on this order, since it was signed by the military commanders and a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I found this order, I saw that it had to do with civilian affairs and the needs of the armed forces as well as the needs of civilians. In terms of the army, the aim is to establish communication, so that this railway line could be used for military materiel and units to be transported to certain regions, so that the railway line would be used both by the armed forces and by the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, when in an order you see the signature of a military commander, whose order is it then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it is stated in an order that a commander issued it, then it is his responsibility. The fact that the coordinator has signed it means that he is aware that he has to cooperate with them, because this has to do with his responsibilities regarding materials, manpower, electric power, so the establishment of the railway line itself is more a civilian undertaking, and the coordinator will have to provide the manpower, the production elements and everything else that is required and that is why he is signing it. But the commander has ordered it, because this was required by the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, this order leads me to some general questions. Can you, as a military expert, say, regardless of what question we are dealing with, if somebody issues an order, or a nomination, if it is signed by military commanders -- a military commander or military commanders -- whose order is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the order of the commander who signed the order. Orders can be issued only by commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, for example, irrespective of this document, there is an order signed by a commander with the signature of a third party, does it change the character of that order by the commander? Is it still the order of the commander, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander who has signed the order is not rid of the responsibility of signing the order. Any third party can be a witness, or somebody who is taking part in logistics or some other function, but the commander is always responsible. It is the commander who has signed the order. There is no -- we must not mix up competencies. The other point is subordination -- the principle of subordination, which states that a superior officer has the right to issue orders to individuals. That is the second principle and it is also stated that the subordinates are duty bound to perform all commands, unless they are criminal acts, so I can be ordered to do something which the commander above me, superior to me, has asked me to do additionally. If this is not a criminal act, I am duty bound to perform what he has commanded me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in your documents I came across several other documents in which several individuals, that is to say, other signatures exist in addition to the signature of the commander. Tell me whether the coordinator who signed this particular order received a military function, or is he superior to a commander -- is that at all possible and is that in keeping with the knowledge you have as a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not think we need comment on military rules and regulations. The system of command is quite decisive on that point. The individual who is here as coordinator is only taking part in this to have it effected quicker, but there is no superior. The commander is the responsible individual and he performs coordination -- if you are talking about that particular order, to ensure everything, to ensure railway traffic. I see that his name is stipulated here, but he has no responsibility -- no, absolutely not. It is the two commanders who signed the order who are exclusively responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier, within your reports you included a document by the commander of the army, General Delic, and it is evidence in this case, and it bears out the fact that the coordinator was not an individual in the military hierarchy. Can you tell us, once again, as this is an important question, Brigadier, whether your expert knowledge testifies to the fact that a coordinator is an individual that exists in military hierarchy, and whether such an individual can be named by a municipal or civilian organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen the document by the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where he states what I in fact say what a coordinator means. That is, it is not a military function and that he does not have the right to issue orders and this kind of individual in the army is not determined. Under given circumstances, for example, if there is a fire and the army comes in to deal with that, and to coordinate the civilian sector with the army sector, then the army might be brought in to extinguish the fire and the police may be called in to see to law and order, but there are no coordinators within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, in the situations you mentioned by way of an example as extraordinary situations, does the coordinator issue orders, or does he only coordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian sector designates him. If the army takes part in a task of this kind, if there is a natural catastrophe or something of that kind, then the commander can be an officer, can name an officer to coordinate those activities. If there are no army forces taking part, then it will be members or the organs of the power in authority, but these are the specific tasks performed by a coordinator under given circumstances to solve a given problem, who is to do what, you know, when there is a natural disaster, then you need the medical corps, you need the police, you need the civilian protection forces, but that is something quite different and the role of coordinators is done by the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Having heard in greater detail questions related to nominations and so on and so forth, and having heard your opinions as to what is meant by "coordinator", I should like to ask you the following: having studied all the documents that were placed at your disposal, and after using all your expert professional and military knowledge, were you able to conclude that this particular coordinator that was nominated by the war presidency was superior to the staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The coordinator in question had no inherence vis-à-vis the armed forces. He could not issue any orders whatsoever with respect to the use of those forces. He was not authorised to do so, because, in the system of control and command, it is only superior officers who can issue orders to the staff -- nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, once again based on your research, was this coordinator a superior to the staff of the HQ of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The HVO is subordinated to Grude, so the line of command goes down from Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, is this command -- was this command on the basis of your research -- coordinator, sorry, on the basis of your research, was he superior to the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That structure, too, has its line of command -- superior to it is only the ministry, so the commander of the municipal staff was not able to issue these orders. It gets its orders from the ministry -- directly from the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the basis of your overall knowledge of this subject-matter, was this coordinator superior to the war presidency, which nominated it -- appointed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that I need comment on that question at all, because he cannot be superior to the war presidency who appointed him. The presidency is a civilian organ at the head of combat preparations and everything -- all logistics, whereas a coordinator is the executor of what the presidency decides. That is how this matter should be understood. There is no superiority vis-à-vis the war presidency of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. May we now go on to quite a different matter altogether -- a new field? When we looked at the preparatory information for the command of the Territorial Defence units, Mr. Esad Ramic for the Operation Oganj, we saw that the document set up five Tactical Groups. Brigadier, were these Tactical Groups completely separate from the Tactical Groups which were to be formed by the supreme command for other military purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What the staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic did to form Tactical Groups was the result of poor knowledge as to what a Tactical Group in fact means. A Tactical Group is something quite different. You cannot form a Tactical Group from small units -- small-scale units, and this has nothing to do with the Tactical Group that was formed later on for the deblocation of Sarajevo for example, so these five Tactical Groups were very small-scale units -- each sent in a particular direction, so they were not in fact Tactical Groups, but, on the basis of that commander's knowledge, he thought he was setting up Tactical Groups. It was an officer who did not have the necessary military background and did not know better.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May we, Brigadier, return to something that I would like to talk to you about for a few moments now? When we heard Professor Hadzibegovic and your own testimony, we saw that the city of Sarajevo, from 6 April, was under a blockade and was subjected to killings and destruction. Could you please tell me whether, for you as a military man, from the military aspects, was the siege of Sarajevo a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo was the greatest problem that the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to confront, because Sarajevo was the centre in which the State organs functioned, and that is why the Serbian side prepared forces for the attack -- to attack Sarajevo, so that if Sarajevo were taken, it would be questionable as to what would happen to the remains of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as the situation was such, as there were no elementary means of livelihood, no electricity, no food, no fuel, no water, no medicines, no water, there was a shortage of all this, Sarajevo lived through a terrible trauma and it was bombed, there were sniper fires, there was grenade fire, and all this was aimed at introducing panic to reduce the morale of the population and a message to give up and surrender, and that is why we had to seek a way out of this situation, to deblock Sarajevo and to open the paths to humanitarian aid and assistance, the necessary food, and the bare essentials for life to be able to continue. That is why the military leadership made every effort to deblock Sarajevo. These efforts were planned on the basis of internal forces, and what ammunition and arms we had and from the encirclement to bring in the forces necessary and to try to deblock Sarajevo. It was to this goal that plans were devised to set up on the basis of these small units in the municipalities and communes, to determine the various platoons, to make our forces larger, and to combine forces and to try and effect the deblocation of the city of Sarajevo. It was for this reason that, in mid May, the first Tactical Groups were formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you something at this point? What Tactical Groups were first formed in mid May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain what I mean by a "Tactical Group", because we cannot speak of Tactical Groups without knowing what they in fact are. A Tactical Group, according to regulations of the brigades and military encyclopaedia that we used in the war, Tactical Groups imply what a combat group is, what an operative group is, and what a Tactical Group is. Let me say what we mean by a "tactical group". It is of a temporary composition, which will be selected from units, and these are set up when a formation unit cannot solve the problem in hand -- whether we are -- so it is a temporary formation -- whether it is on the front or elsewhere. If we have to liquidate a battalion or a company -- if we send one battalion to do this, it is not enough. We cannot solve the problem by a formational unit and then our regulations provide for the setting up of a Tactical Group, which is stronger than a battalion -- as the commander of a division, or a regiment, I say that I think two battalions will be able to solve this problem, and I resort to the different branches to be able to solve this problem by setting up a Tactical Group, so it is only a temporary formation. It is not a permanent formation. We know what we mean by permanent formations, platoons, companies, batteries, battalions, regiments and so on, but this is a temporary formation which is incorporated into our formations in order to solve a given problem. As outside Sarajevo we had these fragmented forces, fragmented battalions -- the staff tried to conjoin our forces so that the command composition be formed so as to be able to function separately and to have the necessary impact and so this Tactical Group was given a concrete task. We decide who the commander is to be, and who the members of this temporary formation, the officers, are to be, the amount of units which are to form that temporary formation, what the logistics will be and what will be the task that that temporary formation will have to perform, and it is active until the task is fulfilled. Once the task is fulfilled, the formation is dissolved and the units go back to their organic units. So, that is what is meant by a "Tactical Group" as a temporary formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said that, to solve that particular combat operation, the deblocking of Sarajevo, that these Tactical Groups were formed in the middle of May. Can you tell us what Tactical Groups were formed in mid May -- what particular Tactical Groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff of the supreme command set up two Tactical Groups -- Tactical Group 1, and Tactical Group Visoko. They were forces which were to try to deblock the city of Sarajevo, together with the forces of the town's defence -- the town's defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who was the first commander of Tactical Group number 1 -- do you know who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do -- the commander was Mustafa Polutak -- he was the commander from the very beginning of Tactical Group 1 and the chief of staff was Major Sucro Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the HQ of the Tactical Group was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Tactical Group was in Pazaric. It is some 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Brigadier, whether at that time, after the formation of Tactical Group 1 and Tactical Group Visoko, were there any attempts to deblock the city of Sarajevo by combining the activities of these tactical units and the outside units as well, and those inside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as the order was given to form these groups in mid May, they started preparations -- units from the Pazaric region arrived. This lasted for several days. They were equipped with armaments and ammunition and food, and everything had to be in place for the soldiers to be able to perform their tasks. The fighting lasted from 12 to 18 June, so from May, which was the time that they were formed, about one month elapsed, so there was a month of preparation, whereas the combat operations began on 12 June and went on up to 18 June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, who made up the composition of a Tactical Group 1, whose commander was Colonel Mustafa Polutak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me refer back to the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the chart together. It is annex VI/2. That is the diagram. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain on the basis of the chart which forces made up the composition of Tactical Group 1 when it came into existence, after it was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The composition of Tactical Group 1 was as follows -- in November 1992, it was directly under the command of the staff of the supreme command of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has an objection to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I make the same objection as I did before, that I have no objection to the Brigadier saying that this is a document which he relied on, but I object to him asserting that the document is correct or asserting the document is true as to its contents, because it was drawn up and prepared by Mr. Polutak. I think there was an attempt once before to tender this document, if I remember correctly, and your Honours ruled it was inadmissible unless the author, Mustafa Polutak, appeared and gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think, your Honours, that it is quite clear that the documents that the Brigadier did not take part in personally -- we are not offering up from the aspects of truthfulness, but from the aspects of factual evidence, that is, that these documents were used by the Brigadier and relied on by him when he drew up his report and in presenting his testimony. Therefore, I just ask that the Brigadier tell us what he thinks about this chart and whether he based his assumptions as to the composition of those Tactical Groups on that chart. That is all we wish to ascertain in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are both saying the same thing, so there is no disagreement here. It is not -- he is not making any claim about the truth of it. I think the objection is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether this document, too, was one of those that you relied upon when expressing your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I should like to ask you, without entering into the truth of the contents of this document compiled by Brigadier Mustafa Polutak, will you please tell us whether your research, during which you came across this diagram that you rely on, were these a basis for you to be able to testify in court as to the way in which Tactical Group 1 was formed? Actually, which forces came under Tactical Group 1, in your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this diagram is an objective presentation of the way in which Tactical Groups are formed. The total forces indicated in black consisted of 1,200 men. I wish to say that these smaller columns are the municipalities from which units were taken to form the Tactical Group. It all depended on what the position of a particular municipality was -- how great the danger it was exposed to, should all its forces, all the forces from that territory be sent to join the Tactical Group. In that case, it would have no units to defend itself. So, it was decided, for instance, that the part of the forces that were on Igman, or Trnovo, there was a total of 600 soldiers in those positions -- 300 were transferred to the Tactical Group and 300 remained to defend that location. This is even more visible in the case of Hadzici and Pazaric, where the lines between the army forces and the Serb army were even closer so that this territory could not be abandoned and out of a total of 1,500 fighters, only 400 were taken to join the Tactical Group, whereas the rest remained within the territory of the municipality of Hadzici to protect its positions. The same applies to the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, does such a chart correspond to your professional knowledge as to the way in which units or parts of units are subordinated to a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the rules of control and command, all parts of units sent to form a Tactical Group are placed under the command of the commander of the Tactical Group and that commander is the one who has the power to issue commands. The commanders from the previous units from which the forces were drawn has no jurisdiction over the forces that have been joined to the Tactical Group. Therefore, to command the unified forces in a Tactical Group is exclusively the responsibility of the Tactical Group commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, is it now time for us to adjourn for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. We will adjourn the proceedings until 10.00am tomorrow. Before we adjourn, the Trial Chamber has received some communication from Mr. Olujic suggesting that he is having another co-counsel instead of the present co-counsel, so I do not know what the position still is. We want to be very clear as to what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, a change of co-counsel is under way. We have already notified the Registry of the Tribunal of this, and shortly, as soon as the necessary decisions have been taken, a colleague from the United States will be joining me as co-counsel. Of course, the Defence will not suffer as a result, because this colleague is very well familiarised with the case, so that this Trial Chamber, or the trial itself will not be slowed down as a result of this, and my colleague, as soon as the formalities have been resolved, will assume his duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have been with Mr. Greaves for a very long time and we really do not know why he has changed his mind in continuing with the Defence of Mr. Mucic. As you have fairly indicated, when the normal hearing has concluded, we will hear Mr. Greaves on the issue. Mr. Greaves, do you have anything to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nothing I wish to say in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am very grateful about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves has been a great help. Of course, the defendant has the right to be defended by counsel of his own choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am grateful to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it will be a personal loss. In any event, we will go further into it later. The Trial Chamber will now rise. We will reassemble tomorrow at 10. (At 5.33pm the matter adjourned until Friday, 3 April 1998, at 10am) 20 21 22 23 24 25
